questions.title: Why hexadecimal, and a conversion
questions.prompt:
Information systems can represent numbers in decimal, binary and hexadecimal format. Many software developers use hexadecimal numbers.

(a) Explain one advantage of using hexadecimal numbers.

(b) Convert the hexadecimal number C9 into a decimal number.
questions.answer:

questions.title: TCP/IP layers
questions.prompt: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) refers to a suite of protocols used to send and receive messages over the internet. The TCP/IP protocol suite contains a number of different layers. Name one of these layers and describe what happens within this layer.
questions.answer:
Application — encodes and decodes the message using protocols such as HTTP, FTP and SMTP.
Transport — splits the message into packets, numbers them and records the total, so the receiver can reassemble them in order and spot missing packets.
Network (internet) — adds the sender's and receiver's IP addresses so the network knows where to deliver it.
Data link — carries out the physical transfer of packets between nodes, and between networks.

questions.title: Von Neumann architecture and storage
questions.prompt:
In the 1940s John von Neumann discovered that computer systems could treat instructions as data and, as such, could be manipulated inside the computer's memory while a program is running. This major breakthrough in computing became known as the stored program concept, and is still used in the majority of computer systems we use today. The von Neumann architecture is shown in Figure 9.

(a) (i) Explain the term 'output device'. Provide two examples.

(ii) The CPU cycle carried out to process data and instructions has three steps to it. The first step 'Fetch Instruction' has been completed for you in Figure 10 below. Complete the diagram by filling in the next two steps of the process, labelled (a) and (b).

(iii) The CPU contains a number of registers including the Program Counter and the Accumulator. Explain one difference between these two registers.

(iv) The CPU is often described as the brains of the computer. It is made up of two main components, namely the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and the Control Unit (CU). State the purpose of these two components.

(v) The CPU is the most important component of a computer system and determines how fast a computer can run. Describe two factors that can impact the performance of the CPU.

(b) As well as having main memory, computer systems tend to have secondary storage which allows users to save data such as programs and files.

(i) Sarah is looking to buy a new laptop. So far, all the laptops she has looked at have either magnetic or solid state hard drives. Which type of secondary storage would you recommend? Justify your answer.

(ii) When a computer is carrying out lots of tasks it can start to run out of memory. In some cases, a computer may have to rely on virtual memory. What is meant by the term 'virtual memory'?

(iii) For a school software development project Sarah has to work with classmates to produce a computational artefact for a local business. The group will be working on this both at school and at home. Sarah suggests working in the cloud for the project. Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of working in the cloud.

(iv) As part of the school project Sarah has been assigned the role of Business Analyst. Describe two activities typically undertaken by a Business Analyst in a software development company.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) An output device is any hardware that conveys information from the computer to the user (2 marks). Examples (1 each): monitor, printer, projector, speaker or headphones.

(ii) (a) Decode; (b) Execute (1 mark each; both correct names in the wrong order still earn 1).

(iii) The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction to execute; the Accumulator holds data being operated on. The PC is part of the control unit, the ACC part of the ALU.

(iv) ALU: performs all basic arithmetic and logical operations. CU: directs and coordinates the operations of the computer and tells memory, the ALU and input/output devices how to respond to instructions.

(v) Any two factors, explained (3 marks each): number of cores, clock speed, cache size, bus width, amount of RAM.

(b)(i) Recommend an SSD (3 marks) — faster, quieter, no moving parts so more durable, lower power, unaffected by magnets. A magnetic drive is acceptable if justified on cost per GB and capacity.

(ii) Virtual memory is an area of secondary storage allocated by the operating system to hold data from RAM temporarily, usually when RAM is full. Accessing it is slower than accessing RAM.

(iii) Cloud advantage (3 marks): access from anywhere, collaboration, automatic backup, low setup cost, extra storage. Disadvantage (3 marks): needs internet access, vendor lock-in, subscription costs, limited control, security handled by the provider.

(iv) Two Business Analyst activities (3 marks each): identify areas for improvement and research solutions; write reports and present them to stakeholders; communicate requirements to analysts, designers and programmers; organise staff training and ensure the system fits the business.

    1  def binary_search1(v, L):
    2
    3      lo = 0
    4      hi = len(L) - 1
    5
    6      while (lo <= hi):
    7          mid = (lo + hi)//2
    8
    9          if L[mid] > v:

(i) In the code there is one example of iteration. State on which lines the iteration starts and ends and explain what it does.

    2
    3      if lo > hi:
    4          return len(L)
    5
    6      mid = (lo + hi)//2
    7
    8      if L[mid] > v:
    9          return binary_search2(v, L, lo, mid - 1)

    12

(i) Referring to the code above, describe two properties of recursive functions.

questions.title: A computing milestone
questions.prompt:
The history of computer hardware is marked by significant milestones that have driven advancements in computing capabilities. The six milestones are:

- Turing Machines
- Transistors
- Integrated Circuits
- ARPANET
- Microprocessors
- Personal Computers

Choose one of the milestones and explain its significance.
questions.answer:
Choose any one milestone and explain it clearly.

Turing Machines: the first abstract model of computability; if a problem was computable, a Turing machine could compute it. They were also used to prove that not everything is computable, showing the limits of computation.

Transistors: replaced bulky, unreliable vacuum tubes, enabling smaller, faster and more energy-efficient devices and laying the foundation for modern semiconductors.

Integrated Circuits: orders of magnitude smaller, faster and cheaper than circuits built from discrete components, allowing a very large transistor count on one chip.

ARPANET: the forerunner of the internet; many protocols used by modern networks were developed for it.

Microprocessors: put computing power on a single small chip, leading to rapid advances in personal computers and other electronic devices.

Personal Computers: revolutionised how individuals work, learn and connect; their affordability made information, communication and productivity tools accessible to everyone.

questions.title: An emerging technology
questions.prompt:
Some current emerging trends include: Quantum Computing, Edge Computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), Biometric Authentication and Blockchain Technology.

Pick any one of these and briefly describe one potential advantage and one potential disadvantage it might have on society in the future.
questions.answer:
Quantum computing — advantage: can solve certain problems far faster than classical computers, leading to breakthroughs in cryptography, medicine and climate modelling. Disadvantage: very expensive to build, run and maintain, and its power could break current encryption.

Edge computing — advantage: processing data near where it is generated reduces latency for real-time applications such as autonomous vehicles and remote healthcare. Disadvantage: edge devices have limited processing power and storage, and managing a large distributed network is complex.

IoT — advantage: connected devices enable smart homes, cities and industries, improving convenience and efficiency. Disadvantage: devices collect sensitive personal data and are often vulnerable to security breaches.

Biometric authentication — advantage: fingerprints, faces or iris patterns are hard to forge, giving strong security and convenience. Disadvantage: privacy concerns and the risk of spoofing, false positives and false negatives.

Blockchain — advantage: a decentralised, transparent and tamper-resistant record of transactions. Disadvantage: public ledgers can be traced back to individuals, and mining consumes large amounts of energy.

(b) The Python code below shows an implementation of the bubble sort algorithm.

    values = [50, 70, 30, 60, 20]

    for i in range(len(values)):
        for j in range(len(values)-1):
            if values[j] > values[j+1]:
                t = values[j+1]
                values[j+1] = values[j]
                values[j] = t

    print("OUTPUT:", values)

(i) State the data type of the variable values.

(iii) What does len(values) return?

(iii) Suggest one improvement that would reduce either the number of comparisons or the number of swaps required.

(a)(i) a and b.

(ii) t is a temporary variable used to hold the value of a during the swap. Without it, the value of a would be lost when b is assigned to a.

(iii) Advantage: flowcharts are easier to understand than code, especially for non-programmers; they show the flow and logic visually; they are independent of a programming language. (iii) 5.

After pass 5: 20 30 50 60 70

questions.title: ASCII versus Unicode
questions.prompt: ASCII and Unicode are both examples of character encoding systems. Compare ASCII and Unicode under the headings, memory usage and compatibility.
questions.answer:
Memory usage: ASCII is a fixed-width encoding that uses 7 bits for 128 characters, so it is very memory-efficient for English text; extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 characters. Unicode may use 1 to 4 bytes per character, which can increase memory usage, but it can represent over 1.1 million characters including non-Roman scripts, mathematical symbols and emojis.

Compatibility: Unicode is backward compatible with ASCII — the first 128 Unicode characters are identical to ASCII. Unicode offers far greater compatibility because it supports characters from all languages, so applications in different countries can communicate seamlessly.

questions.title: GCD, recursion and quicksort
questions.prompt:
(a) The Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two integers is the largest number that divides both with no remainder. This code implements Euclid's algorithm using subtraction:

    def gcd(a, b):
        while a != b:
            if a > b:
                a = a - b
            elif b > a:
                b = b - a
        return a

    print("The GCD is", gcd(45, 18))

(i) State the purpose of the def keyword on line 1.
(ii) Complete the trace table starting with a = 45 and b = 18.
(iii) Explain why a for loop would not be suitable for this algorithm.

(b) A recursive implementation:

    def recursive_gcd(a, b):
        if b == 0:
            return a
        return recursive_gcd(b, a%b)

    print("The GCD is", recursive_gcd(45, 18))

(i) Outline the meaning of 'base case' and 'recursive case'.
(ii) Explain the use of the variable b and the expression a%b on line 4.
(iii) Which version would you recommend for very large numbers on a machine with limited RAM? Justify in terms of memory.

(c) Quicksort uses partitioning around a pivot.
(i) For the list 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 with pivot 13, state the two sub-lists after one partitioning step.
(ii) Describe the next steps quicksort takes.
(iii) Outline two common strategies for selecting a pivot.
(iv) Explain the best and worst-case time complexity of quicksort.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) def introduces (defines) the function gcd.

(ii) a | b
45 | 18
27 | 18
9 | 18
9 | 9

The loop ends when a and b are both 9, so the GCD is 9.

(iii) The number of iterations is not known before the algorithm runs; it varies with the arguments. A for loop needs a known number of repetitions, so a while loop is the correct choice.

(b)(i) The base case is the condition that stops the function calling itself indefinitely, e.g. b == 0, where the answer a is known. The recursive case is the part that calls the function again with a simpler or smaller version of the problem and eventually reaches the base case.

(ii) b is the second parameter: it is checked against 0 for the base case and becomes the first argument in the next call. a%b is the remainder when a is divided by b; it becomes the new second argument. This uses the fact that gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), reducing the problem each time.

(iii) gcd, the non-recursive version. Its memory use stays constant because the loop reuses the same variables. The recursive version adds a new stack frame for every call, so memory grows with the size of the numbers and can cause a stack overflow on a machine with limited RAM.

(c)(i) Left sub-list: [10]. Right sub-list: [29, 14, 37].

(ii) Quicksort applies the same process recursively to each sub-list. A sub-list of one element is already sorted. For a larger sub-list it chooses a new pivot and partitions around it, repeating until every sub-list has one element; the sorted sub-lists are then combined in order.

(iii) Any two: first element, last element, middle element, median of first/middle/last, median of medians, random element.

(iv) Best case O(n log n): each pivot divides the list into two roughly equal halves, giving a balanced recursion tree about log n levels deep, with n work at each level. Worst case O(n²): the pivot repeatedly produces very unbalanced splits, such as always being the smallest or largest element, giving n levels and n work per level. This can happen on already sorted or reverse-sorted lists.

(iv) Identify two additional variables that could enhance the model.

(b) "All models are wrong, but some are useful."
(i) Outline one limitation and one benefit of modelling and simulation.
(ii) Explain why abstraction is important when developing a model.
(iii) Pick two of Education, Mental wellbeing, Environment and Traffic management. Briefly describe how modelling could address a problem and improve outcomes in each.

(c) A health agency wants to predict how an infectious disease might spread in a school and evaluate containment strategies.
(i) Describe how agent-based modelling could simulate disease spread.
(ii) Outline one emergent behaviour the simulation could reveal.
(iii) Suggest one strategy the agency could test and explain how its success would be measured.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Test outcome.

(ii) Any two: Gender, Age, Transmission, Instructor experience (years).

(iii) Any two: younger drivers (under 20) tend to fail more; automatic-transmission drivers tend to pass while manual drivers fail more often; more experienced instructors are associated with higher pass rates; the number of females who pass equals the number of males who fail.

(iv) Any two: number of lessons; number of previous attempts; time of day of the test; weather conditions; familiarity with the car.

(b)(i) Limitation: a model is a simplification that omits details, and its assumptions or data may be biased, incomplete or wrong. Benefit: models make complex systems easier to understand, reveal patterns and allow predictions and "what if" scenarios to be tested safely and cheaply.

(ii) Abstraction lets the modeller focus on the essential elements and ignore unnecessary detail. Without it a model would be too complex to understand, analyse or simulate, and less useful for predicting outcomes.

(iii) Education: simulate teaching methods or virtual classrooms to see which improve engagement and performance. Mental wellbeing: simulate stress, social interaction and lifestyle factors to identify triggers and test interventions. Environment: simulate climate or ecosystem dynamics to predict change and guide policy. Traffic management: simulate vehicle flow to find congestion points and optimise signal timings.

(c)(i) Model each student and teacher as an agent with attributes such as vaccination status and infection state. Let agents interact in locations such as classrooms and the canteen, and apply rules for contact duration and mask-wearing to simulate transmission.

(ii) Clusters of infection in high-interaction areas such as hallways; outbreaks linked to particular activities; higher infection rates among specific groups (superspreaders); transmission slowing as people recover.

(iii) Any strategy, e.g. closing the canteen, staggered break times, mask-wearing or isolating infected students. Measure success by comparing the peak infection rate, total infections, or the time for the outbreak to end against a baseline simulation without the strategy.

questions.title: Cache and RAM
questions.prompt: Cache and RAM are both important types of computer memory. Compare cache and RAM under the headings: purpose and speed.
questions.answer:
Purpose: both are volatile memory that temporarily stores data and instructions for the CPU. Cache stores frequently accessed data close to the CPU to reduce access time; RAM stores the larger set of programs and data currently used by the operating system and applications.

Speed: both are fast, but cache is significantly faster than RAM, so the CPU retrieves frequently used data from cache while RAM provides slower access to a larger working memory.

questions.title: Login logic circuit
questions.prompt:
A school system grants access when both the username (A) and password (B) are correct, or when an administrator override (C) is active. A, B and C are 1 when true and 0 when false.

Sketch the logic circuit diagram for this system using the appropriate gate symbols. (Describe the gates and connections if you cannot sketch.)
questions.answer:
The expression is (A AND B) OR C.

Circuit: feed A and B into an AND gate. Feed the output of that AND gate and input C into an OR gate. The output of the OR gate is the access decision.

questions.title: Student records in the cloud
questions.prompt:
A school is moving its student records from a local server to a cloud-based storage service.

(a) Outline one advantage of this move to cloud storage for the school.
(b) Explain one concern the school should consider when storing student records in the cloud.
questions.answer:

questions.title: While loop algorithm
questions.prompt: Construct an algorithm that uses a while loop to display the values 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12. The algorithm can be expressed in a flowchart or in pseudocode.
questions.answer:
Pseudocode:

    number = 0
    while number <= 12:
        display number
        number = number + 3

The loop prints 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12, then stops when number becomes 15.

questions.title: Insertion sort passes
questions.prompt:
A student is applying insertion sort to a list. After four passes the numbers 4, 6, 9 and 12 are sorted: 4, 6, 9, 12, 5, 10, 3, 11. Four more passes are required, and the next value to insert is 5.

(a) Complete the state of the list after each of the remaining four passes.
(b) Outline how insertion sort decides where to place each new element.
questions.answer:
(a) Pass 5: 4 5 6 9 12 10 3 11
Pass 6: 4 5 6 9 10 12 3 11
Pass 7: 3 4 5 6 9 10 12 11
Pass 8: 3 4 5 6 9 10 11 12

(b) Insertion sort takes the next item and inserts it into the correct position in the already sorted part of the list. It compares the item with the values before it, shifting or swapping them right until the item is in place. It repeats until every item is sorted.

questions.title: Why AI makes mistakes
questions.prompt: Some students use AI tools such as Copilot and ChatGPT to help with schoolwork. One argument against this is that, despite good prompts, AI can give incorrect or misleading information, which may confuse students or lead them to learn inaccurate material. Explain two reasons why AI can make mistakes.
questions.answer:
Any two:

- AI does not truly understand the topic; it predicts likely output from patterns in its training data, so it can produce plausible but wrong answers (hallucination).
- Its training data may contain errors or outdated information, which the model repeats.
- Its training data may be biased or one-sided because it was created by humans, leading to unbalanced or misleading answers.
- It has no awareness of the current context unless given it, and may struggle with ambiguous or very specific questions.

questions.title: Modular design
questions.prompt:
A company is developing a program to fully manage a restaurant ordering system for customers. They will use modular design.

(a) Explain what is meant by modular design in software development.
(b) Suggest three modules that could be created for this restaurant ordering system.
questions.answer:
(a) Modular design means dividing a large program into smaller, manageable sections called modules. Each module handles one specific task, such as orders or payments, which makes the system easier to develop, test, reuse and maintain.

(b) Any three: order taking, payment processing, menu management, user accounts/staff logins, reporting, table management, inventory/stock.

questions.title: Universal design in an app
questions.prompt: A company is designing an educational app for secondary school students with a wide range of abilities, including visual, auditory and motor impairments. Describe two examples of how the app could follow Principles of Universal Design, naming a specific principle in each example.
questions.answer:
Any two principles, each applied:

- Equitable use: all students get the same learning content; a visually impaired student can use a screen reader and receive the same information.
- Flexibility in use: students can choose instructions as text, audio or video.
- Simple and intuitive use: clear, consistent menus let students use the app without training.
- Perceptible information: important instructions and alerts are given as both text and audio.
- Tolerance for error: students can undo an action or confirm before deleting work.
- Low physical effort: large buttons reduce the need for precise touchscreen movements.
- Size and space for approach and use: the interface supports zooming and has enough spacing between controls.

questions.title: Heuristics in self-driving cars
questions.prompt:
The algorithms that control self-driving vehicles often rely on heuristics to help them make decisions.

(a) Outline one heuristic that could be used in the context of self-driving cars.
(b) State one limitation of heuristics.
questions.answer:
(a) Any one: keep a minimum following distance based on speed; slow down when visibility is poor; increase stopping distance in wet or icy conditions; choose the route with the least predicted congestion; leave extra space near cyclists and pedestrians.

(b) Any one: heuristics do not always produce the best or correct decision; they use simple rules rather than full understanding; they can be biased by their rules or data; they may oversimplify complex situations; different heuristics can conflict.

questions.title: Turing machine controller
questions.prompt:
Figure 2 shows a simplified model of a Turing machine.

(a) Outline the purpose of the controller.
(b) Explain why Turing machines are considered important in computer science.
questions.answer:
(a) The controller applies the machine's rules. From the current state and the symbol being read, it decides what symbol to write, whether to move the read/write head left or right, and what the next state should be, including when to halt.

(b) Turing machines give a simple, precise model of how any computer can work. They let computer scientists reason about which problems are computable and which are not, and even though they are simple, they are powerful enough to represent any modern computer. They are a foundation of computability theory.

questions.title: Winter Solstice Lottery system
questions.prompt:
Newgrange is a prehistoric passage tomb in Meath, famous for the beam of sunlight that lights its inner chamber at sunrise on the winter solstice. The Office of Public Works plans an information system for the 2026 Winter Solstice Lottery, allowing the public to apply for a place inside the chamber.

(a) (i) Explain the term 'information system'.
(ii) State the names of two components of every information system.
(iii) Suggest two functional requirements (what the system does) and two non-functional requirements (how the system performs).

(b) (i) For each of the three data types below, give one suitable field name and explain why it fits: String, Integer, Boolean.
(ii) Sketch a simple wireframe for the page where users submit their lottery entry details. Include notes outlining the purpose of the main elements.

(c) (i) Compare a mobile application and a responsive website under the headings: user experience and accessibility.
(ii) Explain two validation checks and one verification check the system could use when applicants enter data.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) An information system is software that organises and analyses business data and streamlines day-to-day transactions. More generally, it takes in data, processes it and produces useful information.

(ii) Any two: hardware, software, data, people, processes/procedures.

(iii) Functional requirements (any two): allow users to submit an online application; send confirmation or rejection notifications; securely store and manage applicant details; allow an administrator to review entries. Non-functional requirements (any two): security to protect personal data; reliability and availability during high demand; compliance with data-protection law; scalability for increased traffic; usability.

(b)(i) String: name, email address or home address — it contains letters, spaces and symbols. Integer: age, number of tickets requested or year of birth — it is a whole number. Boolean: agree to terms and conditions, resident of Ireland or over 18 — the answer is true/false or yes/no.

(ii) A suitable wireframe has: a clear heading such as "Winter Solstice Lottery Entry"; labelled text fields for name, email and address; a number field for tickets; checkboxes for terms and residency; a submit button; and short notes explaining each element. Marking rewards a clear heading, appropriate controls, annotations and a submit button.

(c)(i) User experience: a mobile app can feel smoother and faster because it is designed for the device and can use notifications and touch controls; a responsive website opens in a browser, adjusts to screen size, and needs no installation. Accessibility: a responsive website works on phones, tablets and desktops through any browser; an app may need a compatible device and storage, but can include voice input, large text and screen-reader support.

(ii) Validation (any two): range check, e.g. age between 18 and 120; format check, e.g. email contains @; presence check, e.g. required name is not blank; length check, e.g. phone number has the right digits; type check, e.g. year of birth contains only numbers. Verification (one): double entry of the email address and compare the two; a confirmation screen for the applicant to review; a confirmation email so the applicant can check the details.

questions.title: Königsberg bridges and Euler paths
questions.prompt:
Königsberg was built around a river with two islands. Seven bridges, numbered 1 to 7, connected four areas of land A, B, C and D (Figure 3). An Euler path crosses every bridge exactly once without crossing the same bridge twice.

(a) (i) Starting from A, the route 1 → 4 → 5 → 2 → 3 → 6 → 7 includes all seven bridges but is not an Euler path. Explain why.
(ii) Figures 4 and 5 show alternative bridge networks, both containing Euler paths. Starting from C, identify an Euler path from each figure.
(iii) For each land area, state whether the number of connected bridges is odd or even in Figures 3, 4 and 5.
(iv) Deduce one pattern necessary for an Euler path to exist.

(b) (i) Using Figure 6, explain how abstraction is applied to the Königsberg problem. State one limitation of that abstraction.
(ii) Four friends must cross a dangerous bridge at night. Only two can cross at a time and one torch is needed. Times: Alex 1 min, Beth 3 min, Carol 6 min, David 10 min. A pair crosses at the slower speed, and the torch must be returned if anyone remains. Calculate the fastest sequence.

(c) A city council may adopt a system that recommends the most efficient routes using algorithms like those used for the Königsberg problem. Appraise the potential positive and negative impacts on culture and society.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) The route is not continuous: after crossing bridge 6 you are on land area B, but bridge 7 does not connect to B, so it cannot be crossed next.

(ii) Figure 4 from C: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2 (or 2 → 4 → 3 → 1). Figure 5 from C: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2 → 5 (or 1 → 3 → 5 → 2 → 4, or the reverse of one of these).

(iii) Figure 3: A odd (3), B odd (3), C odd (5), D odd (3). Figure 4: all even (2 each). Figure 5: A even (2), B even (2), C odd (3), D odd (3).

(iv) An Euler path exists when every vertex has an even number of edges, or exactly two vertices have an odd number of edges. The path starts and ends at the two odd vertices.

(b)(i) Abstraction turns the real city into a graph: land areas become points (vertices) and bridges become lines (edges). Details such as the river's shape, distances and bridge widths are ignored because they do not affect the problem. Limitation: the graph cannot show practical issues such as travel time, safety, bridge width or walking difficulty, and some real constraints may be missed.

(ii) Fastest sequence (20 minutes):
- Alex and Beth cross — 3 minutes
- Alex returns — 1 minute (total 4)
- Carol and David cross — 10 minutes (total 14)
- Beth returns — 3 minutes (total 17)
- Alex and Beth cross — 3 minutes (total 20)

(c) Positive impacts: easier navigation and route planning; less travel time and commuter stress; reduced congestion; faster emergency response; lower fuel use and emissions; better transport, logistics and urban planning.

Negative impacts: privacy concerns from location tracking; extra traffic diverted through residential or culturally significant areas; over-reliance on algorithms and loss of navigation skills; unequal access for people without smartphones, internet or digital skills; high implementation costs and disruption if the system fails.

questions.title: Greenhouse controller
questions.prompt:
A horticulture company is designing a greenhouse controller with an embedded system to automate healthy growing conditions. The device monitors the environment and controls equipment automatically.

(a) (i) Name any two digital sensors and any two analogue sensors that could be used.
(ii) List two additional outputs, other than those already in the design, that could be used.
(iii) Describe the difference between digital and analogue sensors.

(b) (i) This code is intended to set the fan based on temperature and door state:

    if temperature > 30:
        fan = "ON"
    if door_open:
        fan = "OFF"

Identify one problem this could cause in a real greenhouse and describe a solution.
(ii) Suggest one additional rule using sensors that would maintain healthy growing conditions.
(iii) The system stores sensor readings and the fan state each hour. Describe one benefit of collecting this data and explain how it could improve performance.

(c) (i) State two characteristics of embedded systems and justify why each is important for a greenhouse controller.
(ii) Choose any two stages of software testing and explain how each applies to the greenhouse system.
questions.answer:
(a)(i) Digital: door sensor (open/closed), motion sensor (movement detected or not). Analogue: temperature sensor, humidity sensor, natural-light sensor.

(ii) Any two: automatic window opener, alarm/buzzer, shade blinds.

(iii) Digital sensors produce fixed outputs such as on/off or true/false. Analogue sensors produce a range of values that change smoothly, such as temperature or humidity, so they give more detailed information.

(b)(i) Problem: if the temperature is above 30 and the door is open, the first if sets the fan ON and the second immediately sets it OFF. The fan can switch on and off incorrectly, so the greenhouse may overheat. Solution: check the door first and use if/else, or combine the conditions with and, so the fan is only ON when the temperature is above 30 and the door is closed.

(ii) Any one: if humidity is too low, turn on the misting system; if light is too high, close the blinds; if soil moisture is low, start irrigation; if temperature is too low, turn on the heater.

(iii) Benefit: the data shows patterns and trends over time, such as when the greenhouse is usually too hot. Explain: the company can adjust the fan rules to turn on earlier, detect faults (for example, the fan is on but the temperature does not fall), and improve efficiency and growing conditions.

(c)(i) Any two characteristics and justifications: designed for a specific task — the controller only manages greenhouse conditions, keeping it simple and reliable; part of a larger system — it must work with sensors and actuators; limited hardware resources — minimal memory and processing keeps cost and energy low; real-time operation — it must respond immediately to temperature or humidity changes; low power — it runs continuously; fast response — plants need quick reactions; low cost — makes automation affordable.

(ii) Any two stages: unit testing checks individual parts, such as the temperature-sensor code or fan rule, on their own; system testing checks the whole system with sensors, rules and outputs under real conditions; integration testing checks that sensors, control rules and outputs work together; acceptance testing checks the system meets the horticulture company's requirements.
